In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Know that these things by which Allah, exalted is He, has sworn must have in them either a religious benefit, such as their being clear proofs of the Oneness of God (tawhid), or a worldly benefit that prompts gratitude, or both. Because of what we have mentioned, the scholars differed greatly in interpreting these things, and each one interpreted them in the way he saw as greatest in rank in religion and most beneficial in this world.

As for His saying ﴿By the dawn﴾, they have mentioned several opinions concerning it:

The first: what has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās, that al-fajr is the ordinary morning (al-ṣubḥ), that is, the breaking of the dawn, both the true dawn (al-ṣubḥ al-ṣādiq) and the false dawn (al-ṣubḥ al-kādhib). Allah swore by it because of what occurs with it: the ending of the night, the appearance of light, and the dispersal of people and all animals, birds and beasts, in search of sustenance. This resembles the resurrection of the dead from their graves, and in it there is a lesson for whoever reflects. This is like His saying: ﴿And by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:34], and He said in another place: ﴿And by the morning when it breathes﴾ [al-Takwīr 81:18], and He praised Himself in another verse as its Creator, saying: ﴿Cleaver of the daybreak﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:96]. Some have said that what is meant by it is the whole day, but that it indicated the whole by its beginning, like His saying: ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā 93:1] and His saying: ﴿By the day when it reveals itself﴾ [al-Layl 92:2].

The second: that what is meant is the very prayer of dawn (ṣalāt al-fajr). He swore by the dawn prayer because it is a prayer at the beginning of the day, and the angels of the day and the angels of the night gather for it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:78], meaning that the angels of the night and the angels of the day witness the recitation in the morning prayer.

The third: that it is the dawn of a specific day. Concerning this view they have mentioned several opinions:

The first: that it is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr). This is because the rites of pilgrimage are among the distinctive features of the religion of Abraham, and the Arabs would not abandon the Ḥajj. It is a great day on which a person offers a sacrifice, as if the pilgrim wishes to draw near to God by sacrificing himself; and when he was unable to do that, he ransomed himself with that offering, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 37:107].

The second: that he meant the dawn of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, because He linked it with His saying: ﴿and ten nights﴾, and because it is the first month of this greatly honored worship.

The third: that what is meant is the dawn of Muḥarram, and He swore by it because it is the first day of every year, and at that time many matters begin that recur with the years, such as the Ḥajj, the fast, zakāt, and the commencement of reckoning by the lunar months. It is reported in a report (khabar) that the greatest of the months with God is Muḥarram. And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The dawn of the year is Muḥarram," so he made the whole of Muḥarram a dawn.

The fourth: that by al-fajr He meant the springs from which water gushes forth, and in them is the life of creation.

As for His saying ﴿and ten nights﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: it came indefinite (nakira) among the things by which Allah swore, because these are nights specified with virtues that are not found in other nights, and the indefiniteness indicates a great excellence.

The second issue: they have mentioned several opinions:

The first: that they are the ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, because they are the days when one is generally occupied with this act of worship (nusuk). It is reported in a report: "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to God than these ten days."

The second: that they are the ten days of Muḥarram from its beginning to its end. This is an indication of the nobility of those days, and in them is the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, and fasting on it has a merit reported in the traditions.

The third: that they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. Allah, exalted is He, swore by them because of their nobility, and in them is Laylat al-Qadr, since it is reported in a report: "Seek it in the last ten nights of Ramadan." As for His saying ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: al-shafʿ and al-watr are what the Arabs call al-khasā and al-zakā, and the common people call the pair (al-zawj) and the single (al-fard). The first: that al-shafʿ is the day of sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr) and al-watr is the day of ʿArafah. Allah swore by them because of their nobility. As for the day of ʿArafah, it is the day on which the matter of the Ḥajj revolves, as in the ḥadīth: "The Ḥajj is ʿArafah." It is also reported: "The day of sacrifice is the greater day of Ḥajj." Since these two days are singled out with these virtues, Allah swore by them without doubt.

The second: that the days of tashrīq are the days for the remainder of the rites of the Ḥajj, so they are noble days. The first: the Eid and ʿArafah are included within the ten days, so what is meant by al-shafʿ and al-watr must be other than them.

The second: some of the rites of the Ḥajj take place only on these days, so interpreting the expression this way yields an oath by all the days of the rites.

The third: al-watr is Adam, who was made a pair (shuffiʿa) with his wife. In another report, al-shafʿ is Adam and Eve, and al-watr is Allah, exalted is He.

Allah swore by them because prayer follows faith, and its value and station among the acts of worship are not hidden.

The first: We have explained that His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ has the implicit sense: "and by the Lord of the even and the odd." Therefore what is meant by al-watr must be the one who is lord (al-marbūb), and so what they said is invalid.

[p. 149]
The second: Allah, exalted is He, is not mentioned alongside something else in this manner, but rather His mention is glorified so that He is distinguished from others. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man say: "Allah and His Messenger," and he forbade him and said: "Say: Allah, then His Messenger." They said: As for the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God is odd (watr) and loves the odd," it is not an established report with certainty.

The sixth: none of the created things is free from being even and odd, so it is as if it were said: "I swear by the Lord of the odd and the even among creation," and thus all creation falls under it. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:38–39].

The seventh: al-shafʿ is the degrees of Paradise, which are eight, and al-watr is the levels of Hell, which are seven.

The eighth: al-shafʿ is the attributes of creation, such as knowledge and ignorance, power and impotence, will and aversion, life and death. As for al-watr, it is the attribute of the Real (al-Ḥaqq): existence without non-existence, life without death, knowledge without ignorance, power without impotence, might without humiliation.

The ninth: what is meant by al-shafʿ and al-watr is number itself. It is as if He swore by the reckoning that creation must have, and it is like the Book and the clear exposition (bayān) with which Allah favored His servants when He said: ﴿Taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾ [al-ʿAlaq 96:4–5], and He said: ﴿Taught him the bayān﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:4]. Likewise, by reckoning one knows the times of worship, the days and the months. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:5], and He said: ﴿That you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth﴾ [Yūnus 10:5].

The tenth: Muqātil said: al-shafʿ is the days and nights, and al-watr is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection.

The eleventh: al-shafʿ is every prophet who has two names, such as Muḥammad and Aḥmad, al-Masīḥ and ʿĪsā, Yūnus and Dhū al-Nūn; and al-watr is every prophet who has one name, such as Ādam, Nūḥ, and Ibrāhīm.

The twelfth: al-shafʿ is Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and al-watr is Maryam.

The thirteenth: al-shafʿ is the twelve springs which Allah caused to gush forth for Mūsā, peace be upon him, and al-watr is the nine signs which Mūsā was given, in His saying: ﴿And We gave Mūsā nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:101].

The fourteenth: al-shafʿ is the days of ʿĀd, and al-watr is their nights, because of His saying: ﴿Seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:7].

The fifteenth: al-shafʿ is the twelve constellations (burūj), because of His saying: ﴿He placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqān 25:61], and al-watr is the seven planets (kawākib).

The sixteenth: al-shafʿ is the month which completes thirty days, and al-watr is the month which completes twenty-nine days.

The seventeenth: al-shafʿ is the limbs, and al-watr is the heart, because He said: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾.

The eighteenth: al-shafʿ is the two lips, and al-watr is the tongue, because He said: ﴿And a tongue and two lips﴾ [al-Balad 90:9].

The nineteenth: al-shafʿ is the two prostrations (sajdatān), and al-watr is the bowing (rukūʿ).

The twentieth: al-shafʿ is the gates of Paradise, because they are eight, and al-watr is the gates of Hell, because they are seven.

Know that what the apparent meaning indicates is that al-shafʿ and al-watr are two noble matters by which Allah, exalted is He, swore. All these aspects we have mentioned are possible, and the apparent wording does not point specifically to any one of these things. If a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or a consensus (ijmāʿ) of the interpreters (ahl al-taʾwīl), is established concerning any of them, it is judged to be what is meant. If nothing is established, then the statement must be understood as permissible (ʿalā ṭarīqat al-jawāz), not as a categorical certainty. Someone may also say: I take the statement to cover all of them, because the definite article (al-) in al-shafʿ and al-watr indicates generality.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: ﴿when it passes﴾ (idhā yasrī) means when it goes on, as in His saying: ﴿and the night when it withdraws﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33] and His saying: ﴿and the night when it recedes﴾ [al-Takwīr 81:17]. Its passing (surā) is its going on and its ending, or it may be said that its passing is traveling through it. Qatādah said: ﴿when it passes﴾ means when it comes and approaches.

The second issue: most of the exegetes hold that what is meant is not a specific night but night in general, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and the night when it withdraws﴾ and ﴿and the night when it recedes﴾. Also, God's blessing through the alternation of night and day and the variation of their lengths upon creation is great, so it is correct to swear by it, because in it there is a reminder that their alternation is by the arrangement of a wise Arranger who knows all that is known. Muqātil said: it is the night of Muzdalifah. Thus His saying ﴿when it passes﴾ means when travel is undertaken in it, just as one says "a sleeping night" because sleep occurs in it, and "a wakeful night" because wakefulness occurs in it. It is a night in which the travel (surā) begins at the beginning of it, at the departure from ʿArafāt to Muzdalifah, and at its end, as it is reported that the Prophet (peace be upon him) would send ahead the weak members of his family during this night. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, held that this is permissible only after midnight.

The third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: It was recited as ﴿إذا يَسْرِي﴾ with the yā' (ي) retained. Then he said: Omitting it is more preferable to me, because it is a fāṣila (rhyme-end of a verse), and yā' are dropped from fawāṣil, and the kasrahs indicate it. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs may drop the yā' and suffice with the kasra before it, and he recited:

كَفّاكَ كَفٌّ ما يُبْقِي دِرْهَمًا جُودًا وأُخْرى تُعْطِ بِالسَّيْفِ الدَّما

"Your two hands: one hand leaves no dirham from generosity, and the other gives blood by the sword."

If this is permissible outside the fāṣila, then it is more permissible within the fāṣila. If it is said: Why was it preferred that the yā' be dropped when it is in a fāṣila or qāfiya (rhyme), while the letter belongs to the word itself, so it should remain as all other letters remain and not be dropped? Abu 'Ali answered, saying: The matter in this is that the fawāṣil and qawāfī are places of pause (waqf), and pause is a place of change. So when there is a pause, the sound letters change in it by doubling, by sukūn, and by rawm (partial vowel) of the harakah; so these letters, which resemble the extra (letters of lengthening), were changed by omission. As for the one who affirms the yā' in "yasrī" both in connection (waṣl) and in pause, he says: The verb is not dropped from in pause as it is dropped in nouns, such as qāḍin and ghāzin. You say: huwa yaqḍī and anā aqḍī, so the yā' remains and is not dropped.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿هَلْ في ذَلِكَ قَسَمٌ لِذِي حِجْرٍ﴾ ("Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?") has two issues:

The first issue: ḥijr means intellect (ʿaql), and it was so named because it restrains one from falling into what is not fitting, just as it is called ʿaql (restraint/binding) and nuhyah (restraint) because it binds and prevents, and ḥaṣāh (from iḥṣāʾ, which is control). Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: innahu la-dhū ḥijr (he is truly one of ḥijr) when he is one who dominates himself and controls it, as if it was taken from their saying ḥajartu ʿalā al-rajul (I placed restriction upon the man). On this basis intellect was called ḥijr, because it prevents from the ugly, from ḥajr, which is prevention from a thing by constraining it.

The second issue: his saying: ﴿هَلْ في ذَلِكَ قَسَمٌ﴾ is an interrogative, and what is meant by it is emphasis, like one who mentions a compelling proof and then says: Is there in what I have mentioned a proof? The meaning is that whoever possesses understanding knows that what Allah, exalted is He, swore by among these things contains wonders and signs of tawḥīd and lordship, so it is fitting that He swears by it because it points to its Creator. Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates what we have said: that the oath is made by the Lord of these matters, because this verse indicates that this is an exaggeration in swearing. It is known that exaggeration in swearing is attained only in swearing by Allah, and because the prohibition has come that the intelligent person should not swear by these matters.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days; then whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:203]. Al-shafʿ is the two days after the day of sacrifice, and al-watr is the third day. Whoever holds this view says: Interpreting al-shafʿ and al-watr in this way is preferable to interpreting them as the Eid and ʿArafah, for two reasons:

The first: the Eid and ʿArafah are included within the ten days, so what is meant by al-shafʿ and al-watr must be other than them.

The second: some of the rites of the Ḥajj take place only on these days, so interpreting the expression this way yields an oath by all the days of the rites.

The third: al-watr is Adam, who was made a pair (shuffiʿa) with his wife. In another report, al-shafʿ is Adam and Eve, and al-watr is Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth: al-watr is that which is odd among the prayers, such as Maghrib, and al-shafʿ is that which is even among them. ʿImrān ibn al-Ḥuṣayn reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They are the prayers; among them are even ones and among them are odd ones." Allah swore by them because prayer follows faith, and its value and station among the acts of worship are not hidden.

The fifth: al-shafʿ is the whole of creation, because of His saying: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:49] and His saying: ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ [al-Naba' 78:8]. And al-watr is Allah, exalted is He. Some of the speculative theologians (mutakallimūn) said: It is not valid to say that al-watr is Allah, for several reasons:

The first: We have explained that His saying ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ has the implicit sense: "and by the Lord of the even and the odd." Therefore what is meant by al-watr must be the one who is lord (al-marbūb), and so what they said is invalid.

[p. 149]
The second: Allah, exalted is He, is not mentioned alongside something else in this manner, but rather His mention is glorified so that He is distinguished from others. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man say: "Allah and His Messenger," and he forbade him and said: "Say: Allah, then His Messenger." They said: As for the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God is odd (watr) and loves the odd," it is not an established report with certainty.

The sixth: none of the created things is free from being even and odd, so it is as if it were said: "I swear by the Lord of the odd and the even among creation," and thus all creation falls under it. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:38–39].

The seventh: al-shafʿ is the degrees of Paradise, which are eight, and al-watr is the levels of Hell, which are seven.

The eighth: al-shafʿ is the attributes of creation, such as knowledge and ignorance, power and impotence, will and aversion, life and death. As for al-watr, it is the attribute of the Real (al-Ḥaqq): existence without non-existence, life without death, knowledge without ignorance, power without impotence, might without humiliation.

The ninth: what is meant by al-shafʿ and al-watr is number itself. It is as if He swore by the reckoning that creation must have, and it is like the Book and the clear exposition (bayān) with which Allah favored His servants when He said: ﴿Taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾ [al-ʿAlaq 96:4–5], and He said: ﴿Taught him the bayān﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:4]. Likewise, by reckoning one knows the times of worship, the days and the months. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:5], and He said: ﴿That you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth﴾ [Yūnus 10:5].

The tenth: Muqātil said: al-shafʿ is the days and nights, and al-watr is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection.

The eleventh: al-shafʿ is every prophet who has two names, such as Muḥammad and Aḥmad, al-Masīḥ and ʿĪsā, Yūnus and Dhū al-Nūn; and al-watr is every prophet who has one name, such as Ādam, Nūḥ, and Ibrāhīm.

The twelfth: al-shafʿ is Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and al-watr is Maryam.

The thirteenth: al-shafʿ is the twelve springs which Allah caused to gush forth for Mūsā, peace be upon him, and al-watr is the nine signs which Mūsā was given, in His saying: ﴿And We gave Mūsā nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:101].

The fourteenth: al-shafʿ is the days of ʿĀd, and al-watr is their nights, because of His saying: ﴿Seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah 69:7].

The fifteenth: al-shafʿ is the twelve constellations (burūj), because of His saying: ﴿He placed in the sky constellations﴾ [al-Furqān 25:61], and al-watr is the seven planets (kawākib).

The sixteenth: al-shafʿ is the month which completes thirty days, and al-watr is the month which completes twenty-nine days.

The seventeenth: al-shafʿ is the limbs, and al-watr is the heart, because He said: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾.

The eighteenth: al-shafʿ is the two lips, and al-watr is the tongue, because He said: ﴿And a tongue and two lips﴾ [al-Balad 90:9].

The nineteenth: al-shafʿ is the two prostrations (sajdatān), and al-watr is the bowing (rukūʿ).

The twentieth: al-shafʿ is the gates of Paradise, because they are eight, and al-watr is the gates of Hell, because they are seven.

Know that what the apparent meaning indicates is that al-shafʿ and al-watr are two noble matters by which Allah, exalted is He, swore. All these aspects we have mentioned are possible, and the apparent wording does not point specifically to any one of these things. If a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or a consensus (ijmāʿ) of the interpreters (ahl al-taʾwīl), is established concerning any of them, it is judged to be what is meant. If nothing is established, then the statement must be understood as permissible (ʿalā ṭarīqat al-jawāz), not as a categorical certainty. Someone may also say: I take the statement to cover all of them, because the definite article (al-) in al-shafʿ and al-watr indicates generality.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: ﴿when it passes﴾ (idhā yasrī) means when it goes on, as in His saying: ﴿and the night when it withdraws﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33] and His saying: ﴿and the night when it recedes﴾ [al-Takwīr 81:17]. Its passing (surā) is its going on and its ending, or it may be said that its passing is traveling through it. Qatādah said: ﴿when it passes﴾ means when it comes and approaches.

The second issue: most of the exegetes hold that what is meant is not a specific night but night in general, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and the night when it withdraws﴾ and ﴿and the night when it recedes﴾. Also, God's blessing through the alternation of night and day and the variation of their lengths upon creation is great, so it is correct to swear by it, because in it there is a reminder that their alternation is by the arrangement of a wise Arranger who knows all that is known. Muqātil said: it is the night of Muzdalifah. Thus His saying ﴿when it passes﴾ means when travel is undertaken in it, just as one says "a sleeping night" because sleep occurs in it, and "a wakeful night" because wakefulness occurs in it. It is a night in which the travel (surā) begins at the beginning of it, at the departure from ʿArafāt to Muzdalifah, and at its end, as it is reported that the Prophet (peace be upon him) would send ahead the weak members of his family during this night. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, held that this is permissible only after midnight.

The third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: It was recited as ﴿إذا يَسْرِي﴾ with the yā' (ي) retained. Then he said: Omitting it is more preferable to me, because it is a fāṣila (rhyme-end of a verse), and yā' are dropped from fawāṣil, and the kasrahs indicate it. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs may drop the yā' and suffice with the kasra before it, and he recited:

كَفّاكَ كَفٌّ ما يُبْقِي دِرْهَمًا جُودًا وأُخْرى تُعْطِ بِالسَّيْفِ الدَّما

"Your two hands: one hand leaves no dirham from generosity, and the other gives blood by the sword."

If this is permissible outside the fāṣila, then it is more permissible within the fāṣila. If it is said: Why was it preferred that the yā' be dropped when it is in a fāṣila or qāfiya (rhyme), while the letter belongs to the word itself, so it should remain as all other letters remain and not be dropped? Abu 'Ali answered, saying: The matter in this is that the fawāṣil and qawāfī are places of pause (waqf), and pause is a place of change. So when there is a pause, the sound letters change in it by doubling, by sukūn, and by rawm (partial vowel) of the harakah; so these letters, which resemble the extra (letters of lengthening), were changed by omission. As for the one who affirms the yā' in "yasrī" both in connection (waṣl) and in pause, he says: The verb is not dropped from in pause as it is dropped in nouns, such as qāḍin and ghāzin. You say: huwa yaqḍī and anā aqḍī, so the yā' remains and is not dropped.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿هَلْ في ذَلِكَ قَسَمٌ لِذِي حِجْرٍ﴾ ("Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?") has two issues:

The first issue: ḥijr means intellect (ʿaql), and it was so named because it restrains one from falling into what is not fitting, just as it is called ʿaql (restraint/binding) and nuhyah (restraint) because it binds and prevents, and ḥaṣāh (from iḥṣāʾ, which is control). Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: innahu la-dhū ḥijr (he is truly one of ḥijr) when he is one who dominates himself and controls it, as if it was taken from their saying ḥajartu ʿalā al-rajul (I placed restriction upon the man). On this basis intellect was called ḥijr, because it prevents from the ugly, from ḥajr, which is prevention from a thing by constraining it.

The second issue: his saying: ﴿هَلْ في ذَلِكَ قَسَمٌ﴾ is an interrogative, and what is meant by it is emphasis, like one who mentions a compelling proof and then says: Is there in what I have mentioned a proof? The meaning is that whoever possesses understanding knows that what Allah, exalted is He, swore by among these things contains wonders and signs of tawḥīd and lordship, so it is fitting that He swears by it because it points to its Creator. Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates what we have said: that the oath is made by the Lord of these matters, because this verse indicates that this is an exaggeration in swearing. It is known that exaggeration in swearing is attained only in swearing by Allah, and because the prohibition has come that the intelligent person should not swear by these matters.

[Page 151]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the lands, and Thamūd, who hewed the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh, lord of the stakes, who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein? So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. Indeed your Lord is ever watchful.﴾

Know that there are two views regarding the answer to the oath:

The first: the answer to the oath is His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾, and what lies between the two places is a parenthetical insertion between them.

The second: the author of *al-Kashshāf* (al-Zamakhsharī) said: the thing sworn to is omitted, and it is "We will surely punish the disbelievers." This is indicated by His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾ up to His saying, ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ This view is better than the first, because when the thing sworn to is not specified, the mind goes in every direction, and so it is more effective in instilling fear. Then, when the description of the punishment of the disbelievers follows, it shows that the thing sworn to from the beginning is that.

As for His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: "Have you not seen" means "Have you not known," because this is not something the Messenger could have seen. The word "seeing" is used here for "knowing," because the reports about ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh were transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur). As for ʿĀd and Thamūd, they were in the lands of the Arabs. As for Pharaoh, they used to hear of him from the People of the Book, and the lands of Pharaoh are also adjacent to the land of the Arabs. Report by mass transmission produces necessary knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḍarūrī), and necessary knowledge is like sight in strength, clarity and freedom from doubt. Therefore He said, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, meaning "Have you not known."

The second issue: although His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is apparently addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, it is general to everyone who knows this. The purpose of God, exalted is He, in relating their story is to be a deterrent to the disbelievers from persisting in what led to the destruction of ʿĀd, Thamūd, Pharaoh and his people, and to be an incitement to the believers to remain steadfast in faith.

As for His saying, ﴿ʿĀd﴾, ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: here God mentioned the story of three groups of earlier disbelievers, namely ʿĀd, Thamūd and the people of Pharaoh, in summary form, when He said, ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾, without explaining the manner of that punishment. In Sūrat al-Ḥāqqa He explained what was left vague in this sūra, when He said: ﴿As for Thamūd, they were destroyed by the violent blast; and as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind … and Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities with sin﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 5–9], to the end of the verse.

The second issue: ʿĀd is ʿĀd son of ʿAwṣ son of Iram son of Sām son of Noah. Then they made the word ʿĀd a name for the tribe, just as one says "Hāshim" for the Banū Hāshim and "Tamīm" for the Banū Tamīm. Then they called the earlier members of this tribe "the first ʿĀd," as God said: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿĀd﴾ [al-Najm 50], and the later ones "the last ʿĀd." As for Iram, it is the name of the grandfather of ʿĀd. Regarding what is meant by it in this verse there are several views:

One: the earlier members of the tribe of ʿĀd were called "the first ʿĀd," and therefore they are called "Iram," naming them after their grandfather.

Two: Iram is the name of their city in which they dwelt. Then it was said that this city is Alexandria, and it was said Damascus.

Three: Iram is a landmark of the people of ʿĀd, who used to build it in the shape of a minaret and in the shape of graves. Abū al-Duqayš said: "al-Arum are the graves of ʿĀd," and he recited:
"Therein are the ʾArum tombs, like the humps of Bactrian camels."

Some people criticised the view of those who said that Iram is Alexandria or Damascus. They said: the dwellings of ʿĀd were between ʿUmān and Ḥaḍramawt, which is the land of sand-dunes and al-Aḥqāf, as He said: ﴿And mention the brother of ʿĀd, when he warned his people in al-Aḥqāf﴾ [al-Aḥqāf 21]. As for Alexandria and Damascus, they are not among the lands of sand-dunes.

The third issue: Iram is not declined (diptotic), whether it is a tribe or a land, because of definiteness and feminine form.

The fourth issue: in His saying ﴿Iram﴾ there are two possibilities. If we make it the name of the tribe, then His saying ﴿Iram﴾ is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to ʿĀd, and an indication that they are the first ʿĀd, the ancient ones. If we make it the name of the city or the landmark, then the implied meaning is "ʿĀd, the people of Iram," and then the governing noun is omitted and the governed noun is put in its place, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yūsuf 82]. This is supported by Ibn al-Zubayr's reading "bi-ʿĀdi Iram" with the genitive construction (iḍāfa).

The fifth issue: al-Ḥasan read "bi-ʿĀda Irama" with both words in the accusative, and it was read "bi-ʿĀdi Irmi" with the ra' sukun for lightness, as "bi-warqikum" is read. It was also read "bi-ʿĀdin Iramin dhāti al-ʿimād," with Iram in the genitive construction with "dhāt al-ʿimād." It was read "bi-ʿĀdin Aram dhāta al-ʿimād" as a substitute (badal) for "fa-ʿala Rabbuka," and the implied meaning is: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, making the city of the pillars into rubble?" As for His saying ﴿of the pillars﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: regarding its i'rāb (grammatical analysis) there are two possibilities. If we make ﴿Iram﴾ the name of the tribe, then the meaning is that they were nomadic people who lived in tents and pavilions, in which a pole (ʿimād) is necessary. ʿImād means "pillar," and it may be the plural of ʿamad. Or the meaning of "those of the pillars" is that they were tall of body, likening their stature to pillars. It was also said: "possessors of lofty buildings." If we make it the name of the city, then the meaning is that it has pillars (asāṭīn), that is, buildings raised upon columns. They used to work the columns, erecting them and building palaces above them. God, exalted is He, said describing them: ﴿Do you build on every high place a sign, sporting?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 128], that is, a landmark and a lofty building.

The second issue: it is narrated that ʿĀd had two sons, Shaddād and Shadīd. They reigned and subdued (people). Then Shadīd died, and the matter passed to Shaddād, who ruled the world, and its kings submitted to him. He heard the mention of Paradise and said: "I will build the like of it." So he built Iram in one of the deserts of ʿAdan, over three hundred years, and his lifespan was nine hundred years. It was a great city, whose palaces were of gold and silver, and whose columns were of chrysolite and ruby, and in it were all kinds of trees and rivers. When its building was complete, he set out toward it with the people of his kingdom. When he was at a distance of one day and one night from it, God sent upon them a cry from heaven, and they perished. It is narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qilāba that he went out seeking his camels, and reached the garden of Shaddād, and he took what he could of what was there. His news reached Muʿāwiya, who summoned him and he told him the story. Then he (Muʿāwiya) sent to Kaʿb, and asked him. He said: "It is Iram of the pillars, and a man of the Muslims will enter it in your time, reddish-white, short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his neck, who will go out seeking his camels." Then he turned and saw the son of (Abū) Qilāba, and said: "This, by God, is that man."

As for His saying: ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands﴾, to what does the pronoun in "its like" refer? There are several possibilities:

The first: ﴿the like of which was not created﴾, that is, the like of ʿĀd in the lands, in size of body and intensity of strength. The height of a man among them was four hundred cubits, and he would lift a huge rock and throw it upon the group, and they would perish.

The second: the like of the city of Shaddād was not created in all the lands of the world. Ibn al-Zubayr read "lam yakhluq mithlahā," meaning God did not create its like.

The third: the pronoun refers to the pillars, that is, the like of those columns was not created in the lands. On this view, "ʿimād" is the plural of ʿamad. The purpose of this narration is to deter the disbelievers, since He, exalted is He, has made clear that He destroyed them for their disbelief and their denial of the messengers, despite the particular features they had. So, O disbelievers, if you persist in your disbelief despite your weakness, it is more fitting that you should fear the like of that.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thamūd, who hewed the rocks in the valley﴾, al-Layth said: "al-jawb" is cutting a thing, as one cuts a collar (jayb). One says: "jāba yajūbu jawban." al-Farrāʾ added: "yajība jaybā." One also says: "jubtu al-bilād jawban," meaning I roamed through it and crossed it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: They used to cut through the land and make from it houses, pools and whatever structures they wanted, as He said: ﴿and you hew houses out of the mountains﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 149]. It was said: the first to hew mountains, rocks and marble was Thamūd, and they built one thousand seven hundred cities, all of stone. As for His saying ﴿in the valley﴾, Muqātil said: the Valley of al-Qurā.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Pharaoh, lord of the stakes﴾, its full discussion has been mentioned in Sūrat Ṣād. We say now: there are several views regarding it:

One: he was called "lord of the stakes" because of the abundance of his soldiers and their tent-pegs, which they would drive in when they camped.

Second: he used to torment people and fasten them with them (the stakes) until they died. It is narrated from Abū Hurayra that Pharaoh staked his wife with four stakes and placed a millstone on her chest, and he faced her toward the sun. She raised her head to heaven and said: "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise." So God lifted the veil for her, and she saw her house in Paradise.

Third: "dhū al-awtād" means "possessor of kingship and men," as the poet said:
"In the shade of a king whose tent-pegs are firmly set."

Fourth: Qatāda narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that those stakes were playthings under which they played for his sake. Know that the statement admits all of this. God, exalted is He, made clear to His Messenger that all of this is of the kind by which might is magnified, and that the strength and the multitude did not prevent a great destruction from coming upon them. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾, and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: the pronoun may refer to Pharaoh alone, since he is nearest to it, and it may refer to all those previously mentioned. This is the closer view.

The second issue: the best of the possibilities in its i'rāb is that it is in the accusative position as a term of dispraise. It may also be in the nominative, as "they are those who transgressed" (by way of predicate), or in the genitive as a description of those mentioned: ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh.

The third issue: ﴿transgressed in the lands﴾, that is, they committed sins and tyrannised over the prophets of God and the believers. Then He explained their transgression by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and multiplied corruption therein﴾, the opposite of righteousness. Just as righteousness encompasses all kinds of piety, corruption encompasses all kinds of sin. Whoever acts without the command of God and rules over His servants with injustice is a corrupter. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ Know that it is said: "ṣabba ʿalayhi al-sawṭ" meaning he covered him and overwhelmed him. The mention of the "scourge" indicates that the great punishment He inflicted upon them in this world, compared with what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter, is like the whip compared with all the other things by which one is punished. The qāḍī (al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār) said: He likened it to pouring a whip that repeatedly strikes the one being beaten until it destroys him. When al-Ḥasan recited this verse, he would say: "Indeed with God are many whips, and He seized them with one of them." If it is said: Does not His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ [al-Naḥl 61] require that punishment be deferred until the Hereafter? How then can these two verses be reconciled? We say: this verse requires the deferment of the full recompense until the Hereafter, while what occurs in this world is a part of that and a preliminary of its preliminaries. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾, which was mentioned at His saying: ﴿was a place of ambush﴾ [al-Naba' 21].

[Page 154]

We say: al-Mirṣād is the place where the watcher waits in ambush. It is a form of the pattern "mif'āl" from "rasada-hu," like "al-mīqāt" from "waqata-hu." This is a metaphor for His watching the disobedient for punishment, and that they cannot escape Him. It is related from some Arabs that someone was asked: "Where is your Lord?" He said: "In the ambush." The commentators have several views on it:

One: al-Ḥasan said: He watches the deeds of the children of Adam.

Two: al-Farrāʾ said: To Him is the return. These two views are general to believers and disbelievers.

Some commentators restrict this verse either to the threat against disbelievers or to the threat against the disobedient. As for the first, al-Zajjāj said: He watches whoever disbelieves in Him and turns away from His obedience, to punish him.

And as for the second, al-Dahhak said: "He lies in wait for the people of wrongdoing and disobedience." These interpretations are close to one another.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 89, verses 15–19:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by honouring him and bestowing blessings upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾

Know that the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿As for man﴾, are connected to His words, ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. It is as if it were said: indeed He, the Exalted, is watchful in the Hereafter, so He does not want anything except striving for the Hereafter. As for man, he is concerned only with this world, its pleasures and its desires. If he finds comfort in this world, he says, "My Lord has honoured me," and if he does not find this comfort, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." A parallel to this is His words, describing the disbelievers: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7], and His words: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]. 

This is wrong for several reasons:

The first: the happiness and misery of this world, in comparison with the happiness and misery of the Hereafter, are like a drop in the sea. So if the one who enjoys luxury in this world is wretched in the Hereafter, that luxury is not happiness. And if the one who suffers and is in need in this world is happy in the Hereafter, that is not humiliation or wretchedness. For the one who enjoys luxury in this world may not judge himself to be happy and honoured, and the one who suffers in this world may not judge himself to be wretched and humiliated.

The second: the attainment of blessings in this world and the occurrence of pains in this world do not indicate merit. Allah often extends provision to the disobedient and the disbelievers, either because He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, or by the judgement of what is beneficial, or as a means of gradual enticement and deception. And He may restrict provision for the truthful, for the opposite of what we have mentioned. So it is not fitting for the servant to think that this is a reward.

The third: the one who seeks completeness should not be heedless of the outcome, for matters are judged by their endings. The poor and the needy should not be heedless of the blessings Allah has bestowed upon them, which have no limit: soundness of body, of intellect and of religion, and the averting of afflictions and pains, which have no limit or restriction. So he should not pass a verdict of humiliation upon himself absolutely.

The fourth: the soul has become accustomed to these sensible things. When these desires and pleasures are obtained, it becomes difficult for the soul to detach from them and to avoid being absorbed in them. But when a person does not obtain any of these sensible things, the soul returns to Allah, whether it wishes or not, and occupies itself with the worship of Allah. Thus finding this world becomes a cause of deprivation from Allah. How then is it permissible to judge wretchedness and humiliation in the absence of this world, when that is in fact the greatest means to the greatest happinesses?

The fifth: abundant practice is a cause of the firmness of love, and the firmness of love is a cause of the intensity of pain at separation. So whoever finds the world more abundant and more lasting, his love for it is stronger, and his pain at parting from it at death is greater. The one who is in the opposite condition is in the opposite state. Therefore, the attainment of worldly pleasures is a cause of severe pain after death, and their absence is a cause of great happiness after death. So how can it be said that finding this world is happiness and losing it is wretchedness?

Know that these points are only valid with the affirmation of the resurrection, whether spiritual or physical. As for the one who denies the resurrection entirely, none of these points holds true according to his view. Rather, it is necessary for him to assert with certainty that finding this world is happiness and losing it is wretchedness. But there is another subtle point: sometimes the attainment of a great deal of this world is a cause of killing, plunder and falling into various kinds of punishment, and sometimes deprivation is a cause of preserved safety. On this assumption, it is also not permissible for the one who denies the resurrection entirely to judge the possessor of this world as happy and the one who lacks it as humiliated, for it may become clear to him that the situation after that is the opposite.

There are questions regarding the verse:

**The first question:** His words, ﴿As for man﴾: does it refer to a specific individual or to the species?

**The answer:** There are two views.

The first: it refers to a specific individual. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa and Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira. Al-Kalbi said: he was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf.

The second view: it refers to anyone who is characterized by this description, namely the disbeliever who denies the Day of Recompense.

**The second question:** How did He call the extension of provision and its restriction a test?

**The answer:** Because each of them is a examination of the servant. When provision is extended to him, his condition is tested: will he be grateful or will he disbelieve? The first: he believed that he had earned that honour.

**The answer:** He constricted it for him by making it merely sufficient for subsistence. It is also recited as (فَقَدَرَ) [faqadara] with light articulation, and with doubling (فَقَدَّرَ), meaning he restricted it. And (أكرمن) and (أهانن) are recited with the nun pronounced with a sukun (أَكْرَمَنْ، أَهَانَنْ) in pausal form for those who omit the yāʾ in continuous speech, being satisfied with the kasra in its place.

Know that the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿As for man﴾, are connected to His words, ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. It is as if it were said: indeed He, the Exalted, is watchful in the Hereafter, so He does not want anything except striving for the Hereafter. As for man, he is concerned only with this world, its pleasures and its desires. If he finds comfort in this world, he says, "My Lord has honoured me," and if he does not find this comfort, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." A parallel to this is His words, describing the disbelievers: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7], and His words: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]. 

This is wrong for several reasons:

The first: the happiness and misery of this world, in comparison with the happiness and misery of the Hereafter, are like a drop in the sea. So if the one who enjoys luxury in this world is wretched in the Hereafter, that luxury is not happiness. And if the one who suffers and is in need in this world is happy in the Hereafter, that is not humiliation or wretchedness. For the one who enjoys luxury in this world may not judge himself to be happy and honoured, and the one who suffers in this world may not judge himself to be wretched and humiliated.

The second: the attainment of blessings in this world and the occurrence of pains in this world do not indicate merit. Allah often extends provision to the disobedient and the disbelievers, either because He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, or by the judgement of what is beneficial, or as a means of gradual enticement and deception. And He may restrict provision for the truthful, for the opposite of what we have mentioned. So it is not fitting for the servant to think that this is a reward.

The third: the one who seeks completeness should not be heedless of the outcome, for matters are judged by their endings. The poor and the needy should not be heedless of the blessings Allah has bestowed upon them, which have no limit: soundness of body, of intellect and of religion, and the averting of afflictions and pains, which have no limit or restriction. So he should not pass a verdict of humiliation upon himself absolutely.

The fourth: the soul has become accustomed to these sensible things. When these desires and pleasures are obtained, it becomes difficult for the soul to detach from them and to avoid being absorbed in them. But when a person does not obtain any of these sensible things, the soul returns to Allah, whether it wishes or not, and occupies itself with the worship of Allah. Thus finding this world becomes a cause of deprivation from Allah. How then is it permissible to judge wretchedness and humiliation in the absence of this world, when that is in fact the greatest means to the greatest happinesses?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 89, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! Rather, you do not honour the orphan﴾ ﴿nor do you urge one another to feed the poor﴾ ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, related their doubt, He said: "No!" (kalla), which is a rebuke to man for that statement. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is, "I did not test him with wealth because of his honour with Me, nor did I test him with poverty because of his humiliation before Me." Rather, this is either, according to the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, purely from the decree (qadaʾ) or the predestination (qadar) and the will (mashiʾa), and the judgement which is exalted above being explained by causes; or, according to the doctrine of the Muʿtazila, it is on account of hidden wisdoms which none knows but Him. Thus He may widen provision for the disbeliever not out of honour for him, and restrict it for the believer not out of humiliation for him. Then, when He, exalted is He, related from them that doubt, it is as if He said: "Rather, they have an act that is worse than this statement, namely that God honours them with an abundance of wealth, yet they do not render what is binding upon them regarding it, namely honouring the orphan." So He said: ﴿Rather, you do not honour the orphan﴾. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: Abu ʿAmr read "yukrimūna" (they do not honour) and what follows it with the yāʾ with a dot below, because when the mention of man (al-insān) had preceded, and it was intended as a collective and in multitude, and it is in the form of the third person, "yukrimūna" and "yuḥibbūna" were construed accordingly. As for the one who reads with the tāʾ, the implied meaning is: "Say to them, O Muhammad, that."

The second issue: Muqatil said: Qudama ibn Mazʿun was an orphan in the guardianship of Umayya ibn Khalaf, and he would withhold from him his right.

Know that the failure to honour the orphan takes several forms:

The first: neglecting his welfare (birr), and to this refers His saying: ﴿nor do you urge one another to feed the poor﴾.

The second: withholding from him his right established for him in the inheritance and consuming his property, and to this refers His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾.

The third: taking his property from him, and to this refers His saying: ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love﴾, meaning you take the wealth of orphans and add it to your wealth. As for His saying: ﴿nor do you urge one another to feed the poor﴾, Muqatil said: "nor do you feed a poor person," and the meaning is: you do not command the feeding of him, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in God the Mighty﴾ ﴿nor did he urge the feeding of the poor﴾ [al-Haqqa: 33-34]. And whoever reads "wa-la tahāddūna" intends "tatahāddūna," so the tāʾ of tatafāʿalūna is elided, and the meaning is: "some of you urge others." In the reading of Ibn Masʿud, it is "wa-la tuḥāddūna" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, from the verbal noun al-muḥāḍḍa.

As for His saying: ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: They said: the root of turāth is wurāth, and the tāʾ is substituted for the waw that is pulled (ḍamma), as in tujāh and wujāh from wājahtu.

The second issue: Al-Layth said: al-lamm is tight gathering, and from it come katība malmūma (a compact battalion) and ḥajar malmūm (a compacted stone). The one who eats crumbles the bread-soup (tharīd) and makes it into morsels, then eats it; and it is said: lamamtu mā ʿalā al-khuwān, alummuhu, meaning I ate it all together. So the meaning of lamm in the language is gathering. As for the exegesis, there are several views:

The first: al-Wahidi said: the exegetes say, regarding His saying ﴿devouring greedily﴾, that it means "intensely," and this is a solution of the meaning, not an exegesis. Its explanation is that lamm is a verbal noun made into a qualifier of the eating, and what is meant is the agent, i.e. "eating lāman," meaning hungry, as though they engulf it by eating. Al-Zajjaj said: they used to eat the wealth of orphans wastefully and hastily, so God said: ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾, that is, the inheritance of orphans "lamman," meaning you gather all of it. Al-Hasan said: that is, they eat their own share and the share of their companion, gathering the share of others to their share.

The second: that the property which remains from the deceased is partly lawful, partly doubtful, and partly unlawful, so the heir gathers all of it, that is, joins part to part and takes and eats all of it.

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it is also possible that the reproach is directed at the heir who obtained the property easily and at leisure, without his brow sweating for it, so he squanders it in spending and eats it greedily, a wide and comprehensive devouring, combining all kinds of desired foods, drinks and fruits, as the wrongful heirs do.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love﴾, know that jamm is abundance. It is said: jamma al-shayʾu yajummu jumūman, and this is said of wealth and other things; so it is a thing that is jamm and jamm. Abu ʿAmr said: jamma yajummu means it increases. The meaning is: "you love wealth with much, intense love," thus He made clear that their greed is only for this world, and that they turn away from the matter of the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 89, verses 21–23:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, when the earth is pounded to powder, pounded and pounded﴾ ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ ﴿and Hell is brought forth that Day; on that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾

Know that His saying "Nay" (kallā) is a deterrent for them from that, and a denunciation of their action. That is, the matter should not be like this: greed for this world, limiting one's aspiration and striving to acquire it, relying upon it, abandoning giving from it, and gathering it from any source, whether lawful or unlawful, while presuming that there is no reckoning and no recompense. For whoever is in this state will regret when regret does not benefit him, and will wish that he had spent his life in drawing near to Allah, the Exalted, through righteous deeds and giving from his wealth. Then He explained that when a day comes that is described by three attributes, that wish and that regret will indeed take place.

The first attribute of that day is His saying: ﴿when the earth is pounded to powder, pounded and pounded﴾. Al-Khalil said: *al-dakk* is the breaking of a wall or a mountain, *al-dakdāk* is compacted sand, and *rajulun midakkun* is a man who treads heavily upon the earth. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-dakk* is the leveling of what is raised by flattening it, and the hump of the camel *indakka* when it spreads out on its back; a female camel is *dakkā'* when she is like that, and from this comes *al-dukkān* (the bench/shop-counter), because of its evenness in being spread out. So the meaning of *dakk* according to al-Khalil is the breaking of everything on the surface of the earth, whether mountain or tree, when it is shaken, so that nothing remains upon its back. According to al-Mubarrad, its meaning is that it becomes level and flat, so its houses, palaces and all its buildings disappear until it becomes like a smooth rock. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "The earth will be stretched out on the Day of Resurrection."

Know that the repetition in His saying ﴿pounded and pounded﴾ means pounded after pounding, like your saying "I thought him a door, a door" and "I knew him letter by letter." That is, the pounding is repeated upon it until it becomes scattered dust. Know that this pulverizing must come after the quaking: when the earth is quaked, quake after quake, and shaken, shake after shake, the mountains upon it are broken, the hills are flattened, the valleys are filled and it becomes smooth. That is at the ending of this world. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes, followed by the second﴾ [al-Nazi'at 6–7], and He said: ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing﴾ [al-Haqqah 14], and He said: ﴿When the earth is violently shaken, and the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 4–5].

The second attribute of that day is His saying: ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾.

Know that it has been established by rational proof that movement is impossible for Allah, the Exalted, because whatever is like that is a body, and a body cannot be eternal. Therefore an interpretation is necessary here, namely that this is from the figure of speech in which the *mudaf* (the governed noun) is omitted and the *mudaf ilayh* (the governing noun) is put in its place. Then what is that omitted *mudaf*? There are several views:

First: "the command of your Lord comes," meaning the reckoning and the recompense.

Second: "the subjugation of your Lord comes," as one says, "the Banu Umayyah came upon us," meaning their domination.

Third: "the great signs of your Lord come," because this will be on the Day of Resurrection, and on that day the great matters and the magnificent signs will appear. Their coming is therefore made to be the coming of Him, to magnify the status of those signs.

Fourth: "the manifestation of your Lord comes," because knowledge of Allah will become necessary on that day, so that it is like His manifestation and His self-disclosure to creation. Thus it is said: ﴿and your Lord comes﴾, meaning doubt is removed and uncertainties are lifted.

The first: The implied meaning is: none in the world will punish with the punishment of God the disbeliever on that Day, and none in the world will bind with the binding of God the disbeliever on that Day. The meaning is: like His punishment and His binding in severity and intensity.

The second: The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection none assumes the punishment of God, i.e., the command on that Day is His command, and there is no command for anyone else.

The third, which is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi: the implied meaning is that none of the zabaniyah (angels of punishment) punishes the human as they punish him. The pronoun in "'adhabihi" refers to the human being.

Al-Kisa'i read "lā yu'adhdhabu wa lā yuwthaqu" with a fatha on the 'ayn in both, and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this reading. It is reported of Abu 'Amr that he returned to it at the end of his life, because it was narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited both with a fatha. The pronoun refers to the described human being. It was said that he is Ubayy ibn Khalaf. This reading has two interpretations:

One: None punishes with the punishment of this man, and none binds with chains and shackles like his binding, because of his extreme disbelief and corruption.

The second: None of the people is punished with the punishment of the disbeliever, like His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. Al-Wahidi said: this is the best of the opinions.

The second issue: The "'adhab" in both readings means "ta'dhib" (punishing), and the "wathaq" means "ithaq" (binding), like "'ata'" meaning "i'ta'" (giving) in the saying of the poet:

"Will you disbelieve after death has been warded off from me, and after your giving me a hundred camels in their prime?"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 89, verses 29–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the state of the one who finds rest in the world, He described the state of the one who finds rest in knowing Him and worshipping Him. So He said: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ [and the verses continue]. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: The implied sense of this speech is that God says to the believer: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾. He may address him honouring him, as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, or through an angel. Al-Qaffal said: Although this is in form a command, in meaning it is a report. The implied sense is that when the soul is at peace it returns to God, and God says to it: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ and ﴿enter My Paradise﴾. He said: The use of a command in the sense of a report is common in their speech, as in their saying: "If you feel no shame, then do whatever you wish."

The second issue: Iṭmi'nān (tranquillity) is settledness and steadfastness. There are several views on how this settledness occurs:

One: that it is being certain of the truth, so that no doubt stirs within it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:260).

Second: the soul that is secure, which fear and grief do not unsettle. This interpretation is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "O soul that is secure and at peace." This quality may occur at death, upon hearing His saying: ﴿Fear not and grieve not, and rejoice in the Paradise﴾ (Fussilat 41:30), and it occurs at the Resurrection, and undoubtedly upon entering Paradise.

Third: and this is an interpretation that accords with rational realities. We say: the Qur'an and demonstrative proof agree that this tranquillity is only attained through the remembrance of God. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying: ﴿Surely in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:28). As for demonstrative proof, it is in two ways:

The first: when the rational faculty begins to ascend through the chain of causes and effects, whenever it reaches a cause that is itself possible in its essence, the intellect seeks another cause for it, and does not stop there. Rather, it continues to move from each thing to what is higher than it, until in that ascent it arrives at the Necessary Existent in Itself, the terminus of needs and the end of necessities. When need stops short of Him, the intellect halts at Him and finds rest in Him, and does not move from Him to anything else. Therefore, whenever the rational faculty is directed toward some possible thing and attached to it, it is impossible for it to settle there. But when you contemplate the majesty of the Necessary Existent, and know that all things are from Him, it is impossible for you to move away from Him. Thus it is established that tranquillity is attained only through the remembrance of the Necessary Existent.

The second: the needs of the servant are infinite, and everything other than God, exalted is He, is finite in its subsistence and power, except by God's sustaining. What is infinite cannot be made complete by the finite. Therefore, to meet the servant's need that has no end, there must be the perfection of God that has no end, so that settledness may be attained. Thus it is established that whoever prefers knowing God for nothing other than God is not at rest, and his soul is not a soul at peace. As for one who prefers knowing God for some other thing, his soul is the soul at peace. Whoever is so, his intimacy is with God, his longing is for God, his subsistence is through God, and his speech is with God. Therefore, at his departure from this world, he is addressed with His saying: ﴿Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾. This is a speech that a person benefits from only if he is perfect in the divine intellectual faculty or in abstraction and singling-out (tajrid wa tafrid).

The third issue: Know that God, exalted is He, mentioned the soul in absolute terms in the Qur'an, saying: ﴿and the soul and He who formed it﴾ (Al-Shams 91:7), and He said: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Yours﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:116), and He said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾ (Al-Sajdah 32:17). At times He described it as commanding to evil, saying: ﴿Indeed, the soul is ever inciting to evil﴾ (Yusuf 12:53); at times as self-reproaching, saying: ﴿by the self-reproaching soul﴾ (Al-Qiyamah 75:2); and at times as at peace, as in this verse. Know that the soul of your essence and reality is that which you indicate by your saying "I" when you report about yourself, saying: "I did, I saw, I heard, I became angry, I desired, I imagined, I remembered." However, what is pointed to by this indication is not this bodily structure, for two reasons:

The first: what is pointed to by your saying "I" may be known while this particular structure is unknown, and what is known is not the same as what is unknown.

The second: this structure is subject to change in its parts, whereas what is pointed to by your saying "I" does not change. For I know by necessity that I am the one who existed twenty years before this day, and what changes is not the same as what does not change. Therefore the soul is not an expression for this structure.

And you say: Some people have said that the soul is not a body, because we can conceive of what is pointed to by "I" while I am unaware of the body, whose reality is that which occupies a space extending in length, breadth and depth. What is known is distinct from what is not known. The response to the objection concerning the soul is mentioned in our book called Lubab al-Isharat. Others said: rather, it is a subtle, pure, corporeal substance, far removed from resembling the elemental bodies, luminous and heavenly, differing in its quiddity from these lower bodies. When it becomes interwoven with this dense body, the body becomes alive, and if it departs from it, the body becomes dead. On the first assumption, its being described as coming and returning is by way of figurative sense, meaning management and its abandonment. On the second assumption, that description is literal.

The fourth issue: Some of the early thinkers claimed that souls are eternal, and they argued from this verse, His saying: ﴿Return to your Lord﴾, for this is said only of what existed before this body.

[Page 162]

Know that this statement depends on the question of when this address occurs. There are two views:

The first: that it occurs only at death. Here the argument of those who hold that souls precede bodies is strengthened, though their preceding bodies does not necessarily imply their being eternal.

The second: that it occurs at the Resurrection and the Last Day, and the meaning is: "Return to the reward of your Lord; enter among My servants," that is, enter the body from which you departed.

The fifth issue: The anthropomorphists (al-Mujassima) held to His saying "to your Lord," and the word "to" indicates the limit of an end. Its response is: "to the judgment of your Lord," or "to the reward of your Lord," or "to the goodness of your Lord." The true response, based on the rational principle we have established, is that the rational faculty, through its rational movement, ascends from one existent to another existent, and from one cause to another cause, until it arrives at the presence of the Necessary Existent. There is the termination of ends and the cessation of movements.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾, the meaning is: well-pleased with the reward, and well-pleasing to Him for the deeds you did in the world. What supports the soundness of this interpretation is what is narrated: that a man recited these verses in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and Abu Bakr said: "How beautiful this is!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the angel will say it to you."

* *

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾.

Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: It was said that it was revealed concerning Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Khubayb ibn Adi, whom the people of Makkah crucified, turning his face toward Madinah. He said: "O God, if I have any good with You, then turn my face toward Your city." God turned his face toward it, and no one could turn it back. You know that the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the particularity of the occasion of revelation.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾, that is, join My servants who are brought near. This is a noble state. The reason is that noble holy spirits are like polished mirrors. When some of them join with others, there arises among them a state similar to that which results when polished mirrors face one another, with rays reflected from one onto another, so that in each one appears everything that appears in all of them. In sum, that joining becomes a cause for the perfection of those felicities and the magnification of those spiritual ranks. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if he is of the companions of the right hand, then peace be to you from the companions of the right hand﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah 56:90–91). That is spiritual felicity. Then He said: ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾, and this points to bodily felicity. Since spiritual Paradise is not delayed from death for the blessed, He said: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾, mentioned with the particle of immediate sequence (fa). Since bodily Paradise is not attained except after the Great Resurrection, He said: ﴿and enter My Paradise﴾, mentioned with the conjunction "and" (wa) rather than "then" (fa). And God, glorified and exalted is He, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad, his family and companions, and grant them peace.
